title: Latency-led partial rendering and SDK handoff playbook
content:
Summary:
This note proposes a playbook for a latency-first Hosted API surface that explicitly optimizes for early partial renderability and robust SDK handoff semantics when tool-calling and structured output are involved. Goal: make consumer UX perceptibly faster for interactive apps (chat, assistants, code runners) by: 1) emitting safe-to-render partial frames earlier, 2) exposing client-controlled checkpoints to resume/resume-with-fallback, and 3) defining lightweight tool-proxy semantics so SDKS can orchestrate tool invocation without blocking the main response path.

Why this initiative?
- Many customers measure user perceived latency rather than median token latency. Delivering useful partial results earlier can improve engagement and reduce cancellation rates.
- Streaming + tool calls today either stalls (wait for tool) or forces clients to implement complex stitching logic.
- Structured output (JSON-like responses) usually arrives at the end, forcing clients to wait. By designing partial structured frames and a typed handoff contract, clients can render intermediate UI and optimistically start local actions.

Non-goals:
- Not replacing the full streaming spec — this is an ergonomic layer on top of streaming designed for interactive frontends.
- Not building a full RPC transport for arbitrary sidecar services; tool proxies are intentionally constrained patterns.

User scenarios (concrete):
1) Developer using Redwood-hosted chat to build a customer support assistant. The assistant can present a one-line summary within 200ms and progressively expand, while a background tool fetches account data.
2) An IDE plugin that shows a partial code suggestion as the model composes while a separate tool verifies imports. The plugin renders the partial snippet immediately and greys out the verification badge until tool results arrive.
3) Low-bandwidth mobile client that receives compact intermediate summaries and can opt into the full structured payload on demand.

Design principles:
- Latency-first partial frames: prefer emitting short, coherent fragments that are safe to present rather than waiting for syntactic completeness.
- Explicit checkpoints: clients should be able to request a resumable checkpoint token to replay or resume generation.
- Deterministic reconciliation: partial frames must embed versioning so the client can deterministically reconcile with later frames.
- Tool minimalism: tool proxy calls should be non-blocking by default and surface a typed status along with the main stream.
- SDK ergonomics: provide client SDK primitives that hide complexity (backpressure, resume, schema validation) while exposing hooks for advanced apps.

API surface proposal (high-level):
- New field in streaming frame: "partial_frame" (boolean) + "frame_type" (one of: prose, summary, structured-delta, tool-stub, checkpoint).
- "checkpoint_token": short opaque string the client can send on a follow-up request to resume the same generation or to request a canonicalized final payload.
- "tool_stub": typed object embedded in stream that identifies a separate tool invocation (id, suggested_action, minimal_payload) and a "tool_status": queued|running|completed|failed.
- "structured-delta": a small JSON patch-like delta that can be merged into a growing structured document. Deltas are ordered and include a monotonic "delta_idx".
- Back-compat: fall back to existing streaming if client does not opt into partial_frame semantics.

Behavior semantics (examples):
- Emit short "prose" partial_frame tokens as model generates. Each token includes a monotonic sequence id. Clients render these directly.
- If a tool call is predicted, the initial stream emits a "tool_stub" frame with tool id and suggested args; client can choose to let the platform invoke the tool (hosted) or to intercept locally (SDK hook).
- When tool is invoked by the platform, the stream continues with partial content and includes tool_status updates. When tool completes, a "tool_result_attach" structured-delta is streamed that can be merged deterministically.
- Checkpoint tokens are issued when the runtime reaches a stable prefix (heuristics: model beam stabilization, end-of-sentence, or explicit operator mark). Clients can later request that checkpoint to retrieve a final sealed structured object or to resume streaming.

Structured output rules:
- Use compact newline-delimited frames where structured-delta contains small patches (path, op, value) inspired by JSON-Patch but with a stricter subset (add/replace/remove) and limited path syntax to minimize client complexity.
- Each structured-delta must be idempotent and include the target structure version. Deltas are applied strictly in delta_idx order.
- Final structured payload is emitted as either: full object frame (when finished) or a sealed checkpoint reference the client can fetch.

SDK ergonomics (developer-facing):
- High-level primitives: 
  * StreamClient.startConversation(opts) -> returns StreamHandle
  * StreamHandle.onPartial(callback) // prose/summary partials
  * StreamHandle.onStructuredDelta(callback) // incremental structured updates
  * StreamHandle.onToolUpdate(callback) // tool_status updates
  * StreamHandle.getCheckpoint(token) -> finalPayload
  * StreamHandle.resumeFromCheckpoint(token, resumeOptions) -> new StreamHandle
- Default safety: SDK will automatically merge structured-delta into a local in-memory tree and expose a stable read interface (readSnapshot()) so apps don't need to implement patch application.
- Failover: if a client loses connection, SDK will attempt transparent resume using last checkpoint token; if not available, SDK can request a deterministic re-run with the same seed to reconstruct deltas where feasible.
- Backpressure and rate-limiting: SDK exposes a flow-control callback so heavy clients (e.g., mobile) can request coarser-grained partials (summary frames only) to reduce bandwidth.

Developer UX examples (pseudocode):
- Minimal usage:
  handle = StreamClient.startConversation({model: 'rw-hosted-v1', partials: true})
  handle.onPartial(text => ui.appendChunk(text))
  handle.onToolUpdate(u => ui.showToolStatus(u.id, u.status))
  handle.onStructuredDelta(d => ui.mergeDoc(d))

- Intercepting a tool locally:
  handle.onToolUpdate(u => if (u.suggested_action == 'fetch-account') { let localResp = localAccountApi(u.minimal_payload); handle.sendToolResponse(u.id, localResp) })

Operational & observability needs:
- Telemetry fields to include in platform logs: partial_frame_count, average_time_to_first_partial, checkpoint_issued (bool), tool_stub_count, avg_tool_latency, delta_apply_failure_count.
- SDK should emit client-side metrics: reconnection_attempts, resume_success_rate, delta_validation_errors.
- Playbook for SRE: ensure partial frames are low-cost to produce (no expensive finalization). Add a low-overhead path that returns partial text asap and schedules tool invocations asynchronously.

Compatibility and migration story:
- Opt-in default. Existing clients continue to receive legacy full-stream frames. New SDK versions opt into partial semantics.
- Provide middleware adapter for mid-tier proxies that cannot parse frames: the adapter can collapse partials into a single coherent stream or emit final-only.

Security and integrity considerations:
- Checkpoint tokens are opaque and bound to tenant; enforce short TTL and audit logs for checkpoint retrieval.
- Tool proxies must respect data isolation — if client elects platform tool invocation, platform must not leak sensitive context to other tenants or to logging unless enabled.
- Structured deltas are validated server-side against declared schema when models advertise one. SDKs validate before applying but must treat server validation failures as authoritative.

Risks & mitigations:
- Complexity for clients: provide SDK primitives and a small reference implementation (JS/TS + mobile pseudo-libs).
- Determinism: model runs can be non-deterministic leading to mismatch. Mitigate by issuing explicit checkpoints only at high-stability points; provide re-run path for canonicalization.
- Tool latency still blocks final semantics: emphasize non-blocking tool_stubs and ability to surface degraded UI while awaiting tool results.

Open questions and trade-offs:
1) How aggressive should partial emission heuristics be? (Default conservative, then experimental ramp.)
2) How large should structured-delta payloads be? (Prefer many small patches for progressive UX vs fewer larger patches to reduce framing overhead.)
3) Policy for checkpoint retention TTL vs customer need for auditability.

Next steps (short-term roadmap):
- Spike: implement prototype streaming frames with partial_frame + tool_stub in runtime (2-week spike).
- SDK: ship JS experimental with automatic delta merge + resume flow (3 weeks).
- Experiment: A/B test with Customer Support demo app to measure perceived-first-draw improvements and cancellation rates (4 weeks).
- Security review & compliance sign-off for checkpoint token flow (2 weeks).

Appendix: heuristics for checkpoint issuance:
- Candidate heuristics: stable n-gram prefix across top-k beams; punctuation + low new-token entropy; explicit model-level signal when model marks a semantic boundary. Combine heuristics and expose override flags for advanced customers.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: aim for a minimal surface that produces meaningful UX wins. Expect additional iteration on structured delta format after prototype data.
- Feedback requested on: preferred delta op set (JSON-Patch subset vs custom lightweight ops), SDK callback semantics, and checkpoint TTL defaults.

End of playbook.
